children.text: Stretching about
14km

along Palawan's west coast, this is the longest white sand beach in the Philippines. It is far quieter than El Nido or Coron, making it ideal for an unhurried beach walk with almost no one else around, a South China Sea sunset, and an easy hopping trip to nearby Port Barton.
San Vicente Long Beach is an approximately
14km

stretch of white sand on the west coast of mainland Palawan, between Puerto Princesa and El Nido. Known as the longest white sand beach in the Philippines, it runs almost unbroken from near the San Vicente town center (Poblacion) in the south to Alimanguan village in the north. The beach is broadly split into three sections: Pinagmangalucan Beach in Barangay Agutaya, Enarayan Beach in Barangay San Isidro, and Bocbok/Tacpis Beach in Barangay Alimanguan, known respectively as Long Beach sections 1, 2, and 3.

What makes this place special is how few people you'll find here given its size. The government has designated it a Flagship Tourism Enterprise Zone with plans for large-scale development, but for now the coconut-lined shore is home to only a scattering of modest resorts and fishing villages. You can walk for several kilometers at midday and meet only a handful of people, and because the beach faces west, the sunset over the South China Sea is spectacular.

The sand is a fine, pale golden color rather than the powdery white sand of Boracay, and its gentle slope makes it great for walking, jogging, and cycling. Port Barton, in the same municipality of San Vicente, is only about
1 hour 30 minutes
away by car to the south, making it easy to combine a beach stay with a hopping tour.

This spot suits couples, families, and long-stay travelers who want an uncrowded sea and slow days rather than nightlife or lots of amenities, and it's also a nice place to rest for a day or two on the way to El Nido.
Administratively, it is a first-class municipality about
186km
north of Puerto Princesa, made up of 11 barangays (villages), with a population of about 33,800 as of the

census. Fishing and farming are the main livelihoods, and the name comes from Saint Vincent Ferrer (San Vicente Ferrer). This is the very first Flagship Tourism Enterprise Zone designated by the Tourism Infrastructure and Enterprise Zone Authority (TIEZA). Long Beach looks like one continuous line, but rocky headlands divide the sand into about six sections, and Alimanguan Beach in the north is described as about
2km
long, with Tacpis Beach to its south about
3km
. The total length is also given as either 14km or 14.7km, depending on the source.

blocks.title: Walk the length of Long Beach

children.text: Even a single section is nearly
5km
long, so it's best to walk along the firm sand at low tide in the early morning. Walking a beach with not a single footprint on it is an experience unique to this place.

blocks.title: Watch the sunset over the western sea

children.text: The sky starts turning red around
. The Alimanguan side of the beach, with its fishing boats and coconut trees, makes for especially good photos.

blocks.title: Ride a scooter along the coastal road

children.text: You can rent a scooter for about
a day (fuel not included) and ride the roads that link the beach, rice fields, and small villages. If you'd rather not drive yourself, rental with a driver is also available.
A small rocky lookout with an entrance fee of about
, offering a sweeping view of Irawan Beach and the rice fields. It's a short climb that anyone can manage.

Tours cover spots such as Turtle Point, Twin Reef, "German Island" (Inaladelan Island), and Paradise Island, split into routes A through E. A joiner tour with lunch and snorkel gear included costs about
per person.

blocks.title: Swim in fresh water at Pamuayan Falls

children.text: A modest waterfall near Port Barton where a donation is often requested instead of a fixed entrance fee. It's a great way to cool off after the salt water.

blocks.title: Watch the fishing village at dawn

children.text: Around
, you can watch bangkas returning to the beach after a night of fishing to unload their catch. If you're lucky, you can buy fish on the spot and ask your accommodation to cook it for you.
Alimanguan Beach at the northern end of Long Beach is a sandy-bottom beach break and the stretch with the strongest waves.
January–February

is the surf season when the waves grow, so San Vicente is called Palawan's surf hub, and you can take lessons from local instructors and rent boards right on the beach. Beginners go in with an instructor, and on days when the waves are strong, simply watching is enough.

items.title: Rainy-day itinerary
items.subtitle: Alternatives for days when you can't get in the sea

children.text: Walk the beach in front of your accommodation during a break in the rain. In the rainy season seaweed and trash wash ashore, so just check the condition of the stretch you plan to walk.

Go mangrove kayaking on the Inandeng River in New Agutaya village. It is described as accessible at high tide and free to enter, and a known way is to set out from accommodation on the Turublien Beach side.
Have lunch at your accommodation's restaurant with a fish dish.
Browse the fruit and fish at the town market, and if the weather clears, climb up to the Bato ni Ningning viewpoint for a view of the whole of Long Beach.

items.title: Surf and relaxation itinerary
items.subtitle: January–February, when the waves get bigger

children.text: Head to Alimanguan Beach and book a surf lesson with a local instructor. Early morning has fewer people and less wind.
Have lunch of grilled fish and rice at a restaurant in Alimanguan village.
Relax in a hammock and watch the surfers ride the waves.
Watch the sunset on the northern beach as it sinks between the fishing boats and coconut trees.
It takes about
1 hour 20 minutes
from Manila to Puerto Princesa International Airport (PPS), with daily flights by Philippine Airlines and Cebu Pacific. There are also direct flights from Cebu and Clark.
San Vicente Airport (SWL) is about
15 minutes
from Long Beach by tricycle, but it has only had intermittent, limited service from small carriers, so always check the current flight status before relying on it.
From
March 29, 2026

, El Nido Airport (ENI) has no direct flights from Manila, and only flights from Clark, Cebu, and Boracay (Caticlan) and a few other cities operate. If your route is to fly into El Nido and work your way south, look into flights from Clark.
Cebu Pacific announced that from
October 24, 2024
it would fly the Cebu–San Vicente route four times a week (Tue, Thu, Sat, Sun). However, there are reports that the route no longer appears on booking sites in
, and the Wikipedia route list also marks it as ended, so check directly with the airline whether it is operating before buying a ticket.
San Vicente Airport officially opened in
May 2018
. Its runway is about
long, so only propeller aircraft such as the ATR and Dash 8 can take off and land, and jets cannot operate there.

Make sure you confirm the destination as "San Vicente" so you don't board a van bound for El Nido or Port Barton instead. If you ask, most drivers will drop you right at your Long Beach accommodation.

Puerto Princesa's city integrated terminal moved from San Jose to Irawan in
January 2023
. Be careful not to head to the San Jose terminal mentioned in older guides; from downtown, the Irawan terminal is about
30 minutes
away by multicab.
Reviews as recent as
say some vans to San Vicente depart from the San Jose terminal in Puerto Princesa or from a place designated by the operator you booked with. Be sure to confirm the departure point when you book.
Chartered bangkas run between Port Barton and San Vicente, or as far as El Nido, but fares are high and service is irregular during the northeast monsoon season (
November–March
) when waves run high.
A chartered bangka from San Vicente Port (the pier) to Port Barton is said to take around
45 minutes–1 hour
, faster than going by road. The fare is negotiable, and service varies with sea conditions.
It is about
186km
north of Puerto Princesa along the national highway, taking
3 hours 30 minutes–4 hours
by van. From El Nido it is about
3 hours
away, and many reviews say the road is generally in decent paved condition.
There are few gas stations around the beach, so fill up your tank in Puerto Princesa or in town before you arrive. For a chartered vehicle, ask your accommodation or a van operator.

items.title: Getting there from Manila in one day

children.text: If you take the first flight from Manila to Puerto Princesa Airport and then catch a van to San Vicente at the Irawan Terminal (about
30 minutes
from the airport), you will reach Long Beach in the late afternoon.
The first van leaves around
and the last around
, so if you take an afternoon flight you may have to stay a night in Puerto Princesa. If you book a direct van that leaves straight from the airport, you skip the terminal.
A tricycle from town to Long Beach costs about
per person, and from the airport to Long Beach about
per person (about
chartered).
The beach is so long that getting between accommodations also requires a tricycle or scooter.
The best time is the dry season, from
December
to
May
March–May
in particular has almost no rain and calm seas, making it ideal for hopping tours and swimming, but midday temperatures rise above 33°C, so sun protection is a must.
December–February

is cool and pleasant and is the period when the most European travelers visit. At this time, however, the waves grow larger on the northern Alimanguan side, making it surf season, and sea conditions differ from section to section, so check that day's waves with your accommodation before swimming.
From
June
to
October

, the southwest monsoon (Habagat) brings the rainy season, and because Long Beach faces west, waves run higher and more seaweed and debris wash up on the sand. Palawan is hit by typhoons less often than the central and northern Philippines, but some years do see typhoon activity in
October–December
, so check the forecast. On the plus side, accommodation prices drop by 20–30% in the off-season.

Accommodation is scattered between Long Beach sections 1 and 2, and around Alimanguan. Most are small beach resorts and bungalows with 10–20 rooms; fan rooms start from around
a night, while air-conditioned beachfront bungalows run about
. The town center (Poblacion) has cheap lodges and guesthouses that are convenient for transport but have less of a beach feel. Good beachfront rooms fill up quickly in peak season (
December–April
), so it's best to book ahead.

Meals are mostly taken at the restaurants attached to accommodations or small eateries along the beach. Signature dishes include inihaw (fish grilled fresh over charcoal), kinilaw (fish cured in vinegar and lime), and grilled squid or prawns. Near the town market there are cheap carinderias (local buffet-style eateries) where you can get rice with two side dishes for about
. Many beachside restaurants close by
8–9 PM
, so it's best to have dinner early.

Among the accommodations along Long Beach, Club Agutaya on Enarayan Beach is the best known. It is an eco resort on about 3 hectares with air-conditioned rooms and a beachside restaurant. The Hotel Elizabeth Resort and Villas is described as a large resort close to the beach with a swimming pool and spa. On quiet Alimanguan Beach in the north there are small places to stay such as Victoria Beach House. Rates vary greatly by season and room, so enter your dates and check directly.

Depending on the stretch of beach, there are almost no restaurants, so many people eat lunch and dinner at their accommodation's restaurant. Some stretches have only a general store selling basic goods, and reports say there are no facilities such as bars or massage shops, so bring water and snacks. Fruit and fish can be bought at the public market in town.
San Vicente has few ATMs, and they often go out of service, so withdraw enough cash in Puerto Princesa to cover your whole stay. Card payment is only accepted at a few resorts.
Smart has relatively stable mobile signal, but it's weak in some stretches of the beach. Hotel wifi also tends to be slow, so download offline maps in advance.
Power outages happen from time to time, so bring a power bank and a small flashlight.
The best times to walk the beach are
6–8 AM
or after
4 PM
. There's almost no shade, so you'll tire quickly at midday.
Sand flies appear on the beach around dusk, so apply insect repellent and use a mat if you plan to sit on the sand for a while.
If you're combining this with El Nido, travelling north in the order Puerto Princesa → San Vicente → (Port Barton) → El Nido makes for a natural route.
Helmets are required when renting a scooter, and since fuel stations are scarce, fill up before you set off.
The municipality of San Vicente charges visitors a tourism environmental fee of about
per person (for stays of 1–10 days). Port Barton hopping tours are registered at the tourism desk, and the environmental fee is sometimes included in the tour price, so check your receipt.
A scooter costs about
a day without a driver, or about
a day for two people with a driver. For Port Barton hopping, a joiner tour runs around
at about
per person, and a chartered bangka is described as about
for 2 people or about
for 3–5 people.
Sunset falls roughly between
depending on the season, so claim your spot on the beach about an hour earlier. Many stretches have no shade or restaurants, so bring water, snacks, and sunscreen in advance.
During the rainy season (
June–October
), waves from the west can run high and rip currents can form, so don't go in past waist depth at beaches without lifeguards.
Most of the beach has no lifeguards or facilities, so let your accommodation know where you're headed if you walk or swim far alone.
Many roads are unpaved and unlit at night, so avoid riding a scooter after dark.
Tourism zone development is underway, and some beach sections may see construction or access restrictions. Check for the latest notices.
Collecting or taking shells and coral fragments from the beach is prohibited.

In some years jellyfish appear at certain times of year, and on some days the waves on the northern Alimanguan side are strong enough to break close to shore. Ask your accommodation staff about that day's sea conditions before going in, and keep children in the shallows.
Medical facilities here are basic, so bring a well-stocked first-aid kit and your personal medication, and keep in mind that a serious injury would require travelling to Puerto Princesa.
